newsitem.title: JAPAN: INTERVIEW--SEVEN-ELEVEN JAPAN SNIFFS FOR FOOD FADS.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW--SEVEN-ELEVEN JAPAN SNIFFS FOR FOOD FADS.

text.p: No matter how busy he is, Toshifumi Suzuki, Seven-Eleven Japan Co Ltd's chief executive, always lunches at the office, sampling noodles, sandwiches and box lunches that are possible candidates for the store shelves.
"The biggest challenge to our business is not competing with convenience or fast-food stores but keeping in tune with customers' rapidly changing tastes," Suzuki said in a recent interview.
"All of our executives taste-test potential new food items at least three times a week to keep abreast of what is up and coming," he said.
Although these efforts may have caused company officials to put on unwanted pounds, they have not been wasted as the company reported booming profits in the last business year.

In the 1996/97 business year ended February, Seven-Eleven Japan Co made a parent current profit of 105 billion yen ($889 million), becoming the first Japanese retailer ever to post an annual profit of more than 100 billion yen ($847 million) and joining the ranks of Toyota Motor Corp and NEC Corp as profit leaders.
Analysts say that rising competition, especially from supermarkets that will soon be allowed to operate on a 24-hour basis, will chew away at Seven-Eleven's growth.
But Suzuki thinks otherwise.

"U.S. convenience stores fell into a rut in the 1980s because they only considered the time element, selling the same things you can get in a supermarket, only around the clock," Suzuki said. "Charisma is important for success in retailing."
The top money spinner for Japan's biggest convenience store chain is prepared foods, which Seven-Eleven makes on its own.
The firm creates new menus using data it has tracked for the past 10 years from outlets across Japan, which now number 7,000 and are growing at the rate of 500 per year.
Soft drinks, snacks and fast food accounted for over 60 percent of the company's 263 billion yen ($2.22 billion) in sales in 1996/97.
Customers can also pay utility and phone bills and buy insurance policies at the neighbourhood "combini", as convenience stores are called in Japan.

"We are more interested in the size of the market than in profit margins. We wouldn't offer to help pay utility bills otherwise," Suzuki said. "Every month over four million customers, which is quite a lot, come to Seven-Eleven stores to make use of such services."
Bolstered by the success of its stores, Seven-Eleven and group firm Ito Yokado Co Ltd, a supermarket chain operator, acquired a majority shareholding in Southland Corp in 1991.
Seven-Eleven Japan plans to restructure the U.S. company, which started the Seven-Eleven chain in the United States and later licensed a franchise to Seven-Eleven Japan in 1973.

When it comes to new business opportunities, however, Suzuki said Seven-Eleven and other firms in the Ito Yokado group have been very cautious. Deregulation is poised to free up opportunities in fields from finance to pharmaceuticals, but the firm shows lukewarm interest in pursuing them.
Starting in April 1998, non-bank entities will be allowed to exchange currencies and industry watchers have speculated that convenience stores will pounce on the opportunity.

"It would be convenient, yes, but changing money is not an everyday need," said Hidetoshi Akiyama, general manager of public relations at Seven-Eleven. "The effort to educate clerks in foreign exchange and to devise safety measures to prevent robberies may not make the business worthwhile."
Suzuki said that he saw potential in the deregulation of the pharmaceuticals sector, although he remained cautious.

Analysts have said one of the first items to be liberalised in April 1998 would be tonics and medicinal drinks which have the potential to lift Seven-Eleven's sales by as much as three percent. Aspirin and stomach medicines could follow eventually.
Nevertheless, Suzuki said, "Just because something is allowed one day doesn't mean it will be profitable.
"Demand has to be great enough to steer customers away from old habits such as buying airline tickets from a travel agent or train tickets at a station, which is a hard task," he said. ($1=118 yen)
